overall: A curious, warm, quietly satisfied read, like a local telling you how the city found its leaks. It starts low and dry, opens up through the satellite idea and the payoff, then settles lower and more certain at the end.

lines.text: Under a street in Arlington, a water main is leaking. A leak technician listens, and hears nothing.
lines.intent: opens cold on the image, setting the problem
lines.note: Weight on 'hears nothing', dry and plain, a small smile in the voice.

lines.text: A leak that stays underground can go unnoticed for weeks or even months.
lines.note: Weight on 'weeks or even months', unhurried.

lines.text: Arlington's water utility looks after 1,470 miles of water mains. Before satellites, it mostly relied on residents to report water flowing where it shouldn't be.
lines.intent: sets the scale and the old way
lines.note: Land 1,470 flat, then ease into 'relied on residents'.

lines.text: Then a team of three went out to listen. They place acoustic gear on valves and over the lines, and triangulate a suspected leak. That is three people for 1,470 miles of main.
lines.intent: the small crew and the arithmetic
lines.note: Weight on 'three', let the final sentence land lower, quietly wry.

lines.text: So the city tried looking down from orbit. In a pilot, a company called ASTERRA scans the entire city with satellites, for moisture and temperature underground.
lines.note: Slight lift on 'orbit', curiosity opening up.

lines.text: The company says its radar looks for the unique signature of drinking water. The city says the technology once looked for water on Mars.
lines.intent: a bit of wonder about the radar
lines.note: Weight on 'Mars', delivered with a half smile, not a punchline.

lines.text: Then an algorithm turns that scan into points of interest. Each one is a pin on the crew's map, a place to go check.
lines.intent: how the scan becomes a usable pin

lines.text: By last November, ASTERRA had handed the city about 340 of those pins. They led to 34 leaks detected and repaired. A pin is not a leak. A crew still drives out to confirm it and repair it.
lines.intent: the honest numbers and the caveat
lines.note: Numbers plain, then drop low and certain on 'A pin is not a leak'.

lines.text: In July, the utility also tested a second program, Paradigm. Its people check the satellite data against a map of valves and hydrants. One pilot runs on an algorithm. The other runs on people.
lines.intent: introduce the second program and contrast
lines.note: Weight on 'algorithm' versus 'people', a clear parallel.

lines.text: When the city tested Paradigm, 7 out of 10 points had leaks. It has helped locate 33 city leaks.
lines.note: Weight on '7 out of 10', steady, no rise.

lines.text: The city estimates ASTERRA saved 1,130,567 gallons of water, and $440,800 in lost water costs. Its conservation supervisor says satellite programs prevent the team from spending entire days searching for leaks.
lines.intent: the payoff in water and dollars
lines.note: Warm satisfaction on the figures, then level on the supervisor's quote.

lines.text: The utility's year-end report adds a finder that doesn't orbit. Splash, a leak detection dog, sniffs for small amounts of chlorine.
lines.intent: a light aside with the dog

lines.text: As of last November, both pilots were under evaluation for permanent use. The satellite points. The crew still digs.
lines.intent: quiet landing and the closing line
lines.note: Slow and certain, the quietest line of the piece, weight on 'The crew still digs'.
